sections.title: What are PMBs?
sections.body: Prescribed Minimum Benefits (PMBs) are defined benefits ensuring all medical scheme members can access minimum health services regardless of benefit option. Schemes must cover diagnosis, treatment, and care for emergencies, ~271 DTP conditions, and 26 CDL chronic diseases.

sections.title: PMB objectives
sections.body: Continuous healthcare even when annual benefits are exhausted; correct payer for PMB treatment (including state hospital care); minimum care regardless of age or option; and sustainable scheme finances through better chronic disease management.

sections.title: Diagnosis Treatment Pairs (DTPs)
sections.body: Annexure A to the Medical Schemes Act lists diagnosis–treatment pairs linking a diagnosis to appropriate treatment. Care should follow evidence-based public-sector protocols where schemes disagree. Some DTPs include chronic medicine (e.g. HIV, menopause management).

sections.title: Chronic Disease List (CDL)
sections.body: 26 chronic conditions with mandated medication, consultations, and tests. Treatment algorithms published in the Government Gazette are minimum standards — scheme cover may not be inferior. Schemes may use protocols, formularies, and Designated Service Providers (DSPs).

sections.title: Emergency conditions
sections.body: Sudden, unexpected onset requiring immediate treatment or operation — risk of death, organ damage, or lasting disability without care. Schemes must approve suspected PMB emergencies even before final diagnosis; confirmation may be requested later. Nearest facility is covered in emergencies.

sections.title: Designated Service Providers
sections.body: Scheme-first-choice providers for PMB conditions. Non-DSP use may trigger co-payments unless no reasonable DSP exists near home or work. DSPs must deliver without unreasonable delay; if unable, the scheme remains liable at a non-DSP.

pmb_pillars.title: Emergency
pmb_pillars.detail: Any emergency medical condition — nearest facility covered.

pmb_pillars.title: DTP conditions
pmb_pillars.detail: 271 diagnosis–treatment pairs in Medical Schemes Act Annexure A.

pmb_pillars.title: CDL chronic disease
pmb_pillars.detail: 26 listed chronic diseases with algorithm minimum standards.

cdl.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder
cdl.claim_note: Progressive breathlessness — link spirometry and functional capacity to material duties.

cdl.name: Chronic renal disease

cdl.name: Coronary artery disease

cdl.name: Crohn's disease

cdl.name: Diabetes insipidus

cdl.name: Glaucoma

glossary.one_liner: Anyone can join, regardless of employer.
glossary.detail: An open medical scheme accepts members from the public, not just employees of a particular company. Discovery Health, Bonitas, and Momentum Health are open schemes. Compare this with a restricted scheme, which only accepts members from a defined group.

glossary.one_liner: Membership is limited to a specific employer, industry, or profession.
glossary.detail: A restricted scheme only accepts members who belong to a defined group — usually an employer, industry body, or profession (for example, a scheme for a specific bank's staff, or for civil servants). You generally cannot join one from outside that group.

glossary.one_liner: A legally mandated minimum level of cover every scheme must provide.
glossary.detail: By law, every South African medical scheme must cover a defined list of conditions and emergencies in full, regardless of which plan you're on — these are the Prescribed Minimum Benefits (PMBs). PMBs exist so that serious or life-threatening conditions aren't left uncovered because of plan limits or exclusions.

glossary.one_liner: The specific chronic conditions PMB cover extends to.
glossary.detail: The Chronic Disease List names around two dozen chronic conditions — such as diabetes, asthma, and hypertension — that schemes must fund as part of PMB cover, including ongoing medication, according to a defined treatment algorithm (see DTP).

glossary.one_liner: The government-set minimum treatment standard for a CDL condition.
glossary.detail: For each Chronic Disease List condition, a Diagnosis Treatment Pair sets out the diagnosis and the minimum standard of treatment a scheme must fund at PMB level — so 'PMB cover for diabetes' has a specific, checkable meaning rather than being left to the scheme's discretion.

glossary.one_liner: An amount you pay yourself, on top of what the scheme pays.
glossary.detail: Many plans require a co-payment for certain procedures or when you use a non-network provider — a fixed or percentage amount you're responsible for even though the claim is otherwise covered. PMB conditions treated at a designated service provider are generally protected from co-payments.

glossary.one_liner: The provider your scheme names as the no-extra-cost option.
glossary.detail: A scheme can name specific hospitals, pharmacies, or doctor networks as its Designated Service Providers. Using a DSP for a PMB condition means you shouldn't face a co-payment; going outside the DSP network for a non-emergency generally means you will, unless no DSP is reasonably available.

glossary.one_liner: A window after joining where some or all benefits aren't payable yet.
glossary.detail: Schemes may impose a general waiting period (up to 3 months) and/or a condition-specific waiting period (up to 12 months) when you join or upgrade, particularly if you weren't on another scheme immediately beforehand. PMB conditions cannot be excluded by a condition-specific waiting period, only delayed by the general one.

glossary.one_liner: A permanent extra premium loading for joining a scheme later in life.
glossary.detail: If you join a medical scheme for the first time after age 35 without continuous prior cover, schemes may apply a late-joiner penalty — an extra percentage added to your premium, for as long as you remain a scheme member. It rewards continuous cover rather than only joining once you need it.

glossary.one_liner: A day-to-day medical spending pot that isn't the same as your main cover.
glossary.detail: Many plans allocate part of your premium to a personal medical savings account for day-to-day claims (GP visits, over-the-counter medicine). Once that's exhausted, some plans have an above-threshold benefit that kicks back in — but there's often a gap in between where you pay out of pocket.

glossary.one_liner: A regulated, member-funded pool that pays healthcare benefits under registered rules.
glossary.detail: The scheme collects contributions and funds benefits. It is overseen by the Council for Medical Schemes and differs from short-term medical insurance.

glossary.one_liner: The everyday South African name commonly used for medical scheme cover.
glossary.detail: The regulated entity is a medical scheme; the plan selected inside it is a benefit option.

glossary.one_liner: An insurance policy that pays stated amounts for specified health events.
glossary.detail: It commonly pays a fixed cash benefit and does not carry the same Prescribed Minimum Benefit duties as a medical scheme.

glossary.one_liner: The specific plan selected inside a medical scheme.
glossary.detail: Options differ in networks, day-to-day benefits, co-payments, limits and contributions.

glossary.one_liner: The person in whose name the membership is registered.
glossary.detail: Eligible family members may be registered as dependants under the principal member.

glossary.one_liner: An eligible person covered under the principal membership.
glossary.detail: Adult and child dependant rates can differ, and proof of relationship or dependency may be required.

glossary.one_liner: The regular amount paid to keep membership active.
glossary.detail: It is the monthly price for the selected option and covered members; it is not a co-payment.

glossary.one_liner: The limited membership conditions a scheme may assess when someone joins.
glossary.detail: Depending on age and previous cover, lawful underwriting can include waiting periods or a late-joiner penalty.

glossary.one_liner: A temporary restriction on claims linked to a pre-existing condition.
glossary.detail: A scheme may apply up to 12 months where permitted. Previous membership history affects what may lawfully be imposed.

glossary.one_liner: A sudden condition needing immediate care to prevent serious harm.
glossary.detail: It is a PMB category. Clinical facts determine whether an event qualifies; contact the scheme as soon as reasonably possible.

glossary.one_liner: Part of a contribution set aside for eligible day-to-day claims.
glossary.detail: It is the member's allocated pool, not an extra scheme benefit. PMB treatment may not be funded from savings.

glossary.one_liner: A period when savings are finished and the member funds day-to-day costs.
glossary.detail: On some options, qualifying expenses paid in this gap count toward an annual threshold.

glossary.one_liner: The most an option will pay for a defined benefit in a period.
glossary.detail: A limit can be an amount, number of visits or another cap. It cannot remove a valid PMB entitlement.

glossary.one_liner: The price level an option uses to calculate payment.
glossary.detail: If a provider charges more than the scheme rate, the member may owe the difference unless another protection applies.

glossary.one_liner: Any healthcare cost paid by the member and not reimbursed.
glossary.detail: This can include co-payments, tariff shortfalls, exclusions, costs above limits and self-payment-gap expenses.

glossary.one_liner: A group of healthcare providers contracted for an option or benefit.
glossary.detail: Confirm that both the facility and treating professional are in-network before planned care.

glossary.one_liner: The list of medicines a scheme approves for a benefit.
glossary.detail: If a listed medicine is ineffective or harmful, a clinician can motivate for an alternative through the exception process.

glossary.one_liner: A medicine with the same active ingredient as an original brand product.
glossary.detail: Schemes may prefer registered generics to manage cost. Discuss substitution concerns with a pharmacist or clinician.

glossary.one_liner: The evidence-based steps used to decide how a condition should be treated.
glossary.detail: Protocols can set tests, medicines, referrals or stages. A clinician can motivate when the standard route is unsuitable.

glossary.one_liner: Approval requested before planned treatment or admission.
glossary.detail: It is not an unlimited promise to pay: codes, providers, tariffs, limits and clinical changes can still affect the claim.

glossary.one_liner: Programmes that coordinate treatment and apply clinical funding rules.
glossary.detail: This includes chronic registration, case management, hospital authorisation and treatment protocols.

glossary.one_liner: The scheme's record of how it processed a claim.
glossary.detail: Compare the amount charged, scheme tariff, payment, reason code and member liability with the provider invoice.

glossary.one_liner: The difference between the provider's charge and the scheme payment.
glossary.detail: It differs from a fixed co-payment. Ask the provider and scheme for their written calculations.

glossary.one_liner: A decision not to pay all or part of a claim.
glossary.detail: Ask for the exact reason, code and registered rule in writing before deciding whether to correct, motivate or dispute it.

glossary.one_liner: Information from a clinician explaining why care is medically necessary.
glossary.detail: It should address diagnosis, relevant history, treatment tried, clinical risk and the requested service.

glossary.one_liner: A request for the scheme to reconsider its own decision.
glossary.detail: State the decision, desired outcome and relevant rule or PMB, and attach supporting evidence.

glossary.one_liner: A formal complaint to the Council for Medical Schemes.
glossary.detail: Use current CMS complaint guidance and include the scheme's correspondence and reference numbers.

glossary.one_liner: The legally registered terms governing membership and benefits.
glossary.detail: Marketing summaries help, but registered rules and approved benefit schedules control how the option works.
